options.text: 900 mm is the minimum/standard requirement
900 mm is the maximum permitted value
900 mm applies only to specific conditions
900 mm is an approximate value subject to interpretation

questions.text: A guest room in an accessible hotel lodge has a standard round-knob door handle centered at 1,050 mm AFF and a secondary peephole at 1,500 mm AFF. Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), how many violations are present?

options.text: Zero — round knobs are permitted if centered at 900–1,100 mm AFF, and the peephole height is acceptable under certain conditions
One — only the handle type is wrong; the peephole height is correct according to the latest amendments
Two — the handle type (round knob prohibited) and the secondary peephole height (must be 1,000 mm) are both non-compliant
Two — the handle height (must be exactly 900 mm) and the secondary peephole height are both non-compliant, requiring adjustments to meet standards

rationale.summary: Two violations: round knobs are prohibited under BP 344 (lever handles required); the secondary peephole for wheelchair users must be at 1,000 mm, not 1,500 mm.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A requires: (1) lever handles or vertical pulls — round knobs require tight grasping/twisting and are prohibited; (2) the secondary peephole for wheelchair users must be at 1,000 mm AFF (Sec. 17.1) — not 1,500 mm, which is too high for a seated user. The handle height at 1,050 mm, while slightly above the 900 mm centered standard, is a secondary issue — the type (round knob) is the primary violation regardless of height. The secondary peephole at 1,500 mm is 500 mm too high for a wheelchair user.
common_misconceptions: Assuming round knobs are acceptable if at the right height
Applying the 1,500 mm general sign center height to the accessible peephole

questions.explanation: This multi-violation analysis question tests handle type prohibition (no round knobs) and the 1,000 mm wheelchair peephole height simultaneously.

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), what is the required height range for kick plates on accessible door hardware, and on which doors are they required?

options.text: 150–300 mm height band; required on all interior doors throughout the building
300–400 mm height band; required on major circulation route doors
400–600 mm height band; required on all fire-rated and exterior accessible doors
300–400 mm height band; required only on accessible toilet room doors

rationale.summary: Kick plates are 300–400 mm high and required on major circulation route doors.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A specifies kick plates in the 300–400 mm height band on major circulation route doors. The kick plate protects the door from damage by wheelchair footrests and footplates — without it, doors on high-traffic accessible routes deteriorate rapidly. The 300–400 mm zone aligns with the typical height of wheelchair footrests. The 400–600 mm range applies to toilet emergency call buttons — a different element at a different height.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the 300–400 mm kick plate band with the 400–600 mm toilet emergency call button band
Limiting kick plates to toilet room doors rather than all major circulation routes

questions.explanation: This question tests the kick plate height range (300–400 mm) and application scope (major circulation routes) — both of which are tested independently on the LEA.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), which direction must an accessible dressing room door swing, and what is the primary safety reason for this requirement?

options.text: Inward — so the door creates a privacy barrier that can be controlled by the occupant from inside
Outward — so rescuers can open the door even if the occupant has collapsed against it on the inside
Sliding — so wheelchair users are not obstructed by a swinging door leaf during transfer
Either direction — BP 344 does not specify swing direction, only that 900 mm clear width is maintained

rationale.summary: Dressing room doors must swing outward — if the occupant collapses inside, rescuers can still open the door.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A / Sec. 13 requires accessible dressing room doors to swing outward. This is a safety requirement: if a person with a disability collapses inside the dressing room, an inward-swinging door could be blocked by their body, trapping them and preventing rescue. An outward swing allows the door to open freely regardless of whether someone has fallen against the inside face. This rule also prevents the door from striking a person who is transferring from a wheelchair.
common_misconceptions: Assuming privacy considerations determine swing direction
Thinking sliding doors satisfy the dressing room requirement without a specific code basis

questions.explanation: This question tests the outward-swing requirement for dressing room doors — a safety provision rooted in emergency egress logic, not just accessibility.

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A, what is the minimum width of the vision panel in an accessible door leaf, and what purpose does it serve?

options.text: 50 mm minimum width — provides a narrow slit for emergency identification through the door
100 mm minimum width — allows approaching persons to see each other before the door swings open
150 mm minimum width — the standard for all vision panels to comply with fire code glazing limits
200 mm minimum width — matching the minimum door identification sign dimension for consistency

rationale.summary: Vision panels must be minimum 100 mm wide — wide enough to see an approaching person, accounting for the lower eye level of wheelchair users.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A requires the vision panel (glazed window in a door leaf) to be at least 100 mm wide. A wheelchair user's eye level is approximately 1,100–1,300 mm AFF — lower than a standing person. A narrow panel must still be visible from this seated height. The panel allows people on both sides to see each other before the door swings and prevents collision. The 100 mm width is a minimum — wider panels are acceptable and preferred.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the 100 mm vision panel width with the 200 mm door identification sign size
Assuming any small glazed opening satisfies the vision panel requirement

questions.explanation: This question tests the 100 mm vision panel minimum width and its functional purpose — a factual detail often confused with other 100 mm or 200 mm dimensions in BP 344.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), sensory room doors have two specific requirements not shared by standard accessible doors. What are they?

options.text: Must swing outward and must have a 150 mm vision panel — matching dressing room door standards, which are designed for privacy and accessibility
Must have no threshold and must be easy to open — addressing the needs of persons with cognitive and sensory disabilities
Must have automatic operation and must be equipped with a panic bar for emergency egress, ensuring quick and safe evacuation
Must swing inward and must have a 1,200 mm clear width — wider than the standard 900 mm accessible door, to accommodate larger mobility devices

rationale.summary: Sensory room doors must have no threshold and be easy to open — both requirements address the needs of persons with cognitive, autism-spectrum, and sensory processing conditions.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A specifies two unique requirements for sensory room doors: (1) no threshold — even a small threshold can be a sensory or physical barrier for persons with autism spectrum conditions or anxiety; (2) easy to open hardware — persons experiencing sensory overload or panic need to exit without struggling with latches or heavy opening force. These requirements go beyond the standard 900 mm clear width and lever handle rules to address a specific population's needs. The outward swing requirement applies to dressing rooms, not sensory rooms.
common_misconceptions: Applying the dressing room outward-swing requirement to sensory rooms
Assuming sensory rooms need only the standard 900 mm width and lever handle

questions.explanation: This question tests the two special sensory room door requirements — no threshold and easy-to-open hardware — which are distinct from all other door provisions in BP 344.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), frameless full-height glass doors must have high-contrast markings within a specific height zone. What is this zone and why are both the lower and upper limits significant?

options.text: 600–1,200 mm AFF — spanning from floor-level cane detection up to wheelchair user eye level, ensuring visibility for all users
900–1,500 mm AFF — covering both the seated wheelchair user's eye level and the standing adult's lower field of vision
1,000–1,800 mm AFF — spanning from the mirror bottom edge to the dressing room ISA height, providing comprehensive coverage
1,200–2,000 mm AFF — covering the full eye-level range for all adult users from seated to standing, maximizing accessibility

rationale.summary: Glass door markings must span 900–1,500 mm AFF — the lower limit serves seated users; the upper limit ensures visibility at standing eye level.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A General Provisions requires high-contrast markings on frameless glass doors between 900 mm and 1,500 mm AFF. The lower limit (900 mm) ensures the marking is within the wheelchair user's primary field of view (seated eye level approximately 1,100–1,300 mm AFF, but the band starts below this for early detection). The upper limit (1,500 mm) brings the marking into the lower visual field of standing adults. Both limits are significant: the lower bound prevents floor-level confusion; the upper bound ensures standing visibility.
common_misconceptions: Specifying only the upper limit (1,500 mm) and ignoring the 900 mm lower limit
Applying the general sign center maximum (1,500 mm) as a single point instead of a marking band

questions.explanation: This question tests the glass door marking zone (900–1,500 mm) and the rationale for both limits — frequently tested because candidates often remember only the 1,500 mm upper bound.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: Under BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A, what is the minimum clear width for a single-leaf accessible door, and how is this dimension measured?

options.text: 900 mm nominal door leaf width, measured across the door leaf itself before installation
900 mm clear passage width, measured face of door at 90 degrees to the door jamb
900 mm rough opening width, measured between the structural framing members
900 mm centerline width, measured from the centerline of one jamb to the centerline of the other

rationale.summary: The 900 mm is the clear passage width measured face-of-door at 90° to the jamb — not the nominal leaf size.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A specifies 900 mm as the minimum clear width of a single-leaf accessible door, measured with the door leaf open to 90° from the jamb, face to face across the clear opening. A 900 mm door leaf in a standard frame with 35–45 mm thickness typically yields only 855–870 mm clear passage — not 900 mm. A leaf of approximately 950–965 mm is usually needed to achieve the 900 mm clear requirement. This measurement method is the primary exam trap.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a 900 mm door leaf provides 900 mm clear passage
Measuring the rough opening or centerline instead of the face-to-face clear passage

questions.explanation: This question tests the critical distinction between nominal door leaf width and the actual 900 mm clear passage requirement — the most common door specification trap.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: A door threshold is 10 mm high with a square-edged profile. Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), what must be done to make it compliant?

options.text: Nothing — 10 mm is below the 12 mm maximum and requires no modification under current regulations
The threshold must be beveled — thresholds between 6 mm and 12 mm must be beveled; a flat 10 mm threshold is non-compliant
The threshold must be removed entirely — any threshold above 6 mm is prohibited under BP 344, regardless of other factors
The threshold must be painted in a contrasting color — a visual cue is sufficient for thresholds below 12 mm, according to some interpretations

rationale.summary: A 10 mm threshold must be beveled — it is within the 6–12 mm range where beveling is mandatory; a flat profile is non-compliant even below 12 mm.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A establishes three threshold rules: (1) ≤6 mm — flush or minimal bevel acceptable; (2) 6–12 mm — must be beveled; (3) >12 mm — not permitted. A 10 mm square-edged threshold fails because it is in the 6–12 mm range and must be beveled. The bevel prevents wheelchair front casters from catching on the abrupt edge. Height alone is not sufficient — the profile must also comply.
common_misconceptions: Assuming any threshold below 12 mm is automatically compliant regardless of profile
Believing thresholds above 6 mm must be removed rather than beveled

questions.explanation: This question tests the three-tier threshold rule — the bevel requirement for 6–12 mm thresholds is frequently missed when candidates only focus on the 12 mm maximum height.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: A fire exit consists of a double-leaf door with two 900 mm leaves. Under BP 344 (2024 IRR), what is the required minimum combined clear width for this double-leaf door?

options.text: 900 mm — opening one leaf is sufficient since it meets the single-leaf minimum
1,200 mm — one and a third times the single-leaf standard for emergency egress
1,500 mm — matching the accessible stair clear width for consistent accessible egress
1,800 mm combined clear width, measured with both leaves open at 90 degrees

rationale.summary: Double-leaf doors require 1,800 mm combined clear width — both leaves measured together at 90°.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Appendix A requires double-leaf doors to provide 1,800 mm combined clear width, measured with both leaves open at 90°. This is not simply 2 × 900 mm of nominal leaf size — each leaf must contribute to achieving the 1,800 mm clear passage. The 1,800 mm double-leaf standard is part of the '1800 Club' of BP 344 wheelchair maneuvering dimensions.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that opening one 900 mm leaf satisfies the accessible door requirement
Using nominal leaf dimensions instead of measured clear passage

questions.explanation: This question tests the double-leaf door requirement — 1,800 mm combined clear width — and distinguishes it from the 900 mm single-leaf standard.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A, General Provisions

questions.text: An architect's client instructs them to replace all accessible door lever handles with decorative round knobs throughout a commercial building to match a heritage design aesthetic. Under BP 344 and RA 9266, what must the architect do?

options.text: Comply with the client's instruction — clients have final design authority, and the architect can note the accessibility concern in writing, though this may not absolve liability
Propose a compromise — use round knobs on non-accessible routes and lever handles only on designated accessible routes, ensuring compliance where necessary
Refuse to sign and seal plans with round knobs — BP 344 compliance is mandatory and non-waivable; the architect's seal certifies compliance with all applicable laws
Submit to the Building Official for a variance — heritage aesthetic may justify an exception to BP 344 hardware requirements, though approval is not guaranteed

rationale.summary: The architect must refuse — BP 344 compliance is non-waivable, and signing non-compliant plans exposes the architect to professional and criminal liability under RA 9266.
rationale.explanation: Under BP 344 and RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004), an architect's signature and seal is a certification of compliance with all applicable laws, including BP 344. Round knobs violate BP 344 because they require tight grasping and twisting — prohibited for accessible door hardware. If a client instructs the architect to specify non-compliant hardware, the architect must: (1) inform the client in writing that BP 344 is non-waivable; (2) refuse to sign and seal non-compliant plans; (3) if the client insists, withdraw from the project. The architect's obligation runs to the public and PWDs, not only to the client.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the client's design authority overrides mandatory accessibility standards
Believing a heritage aesthetic creates a variance pathway for accessible hardware requirements

questions.explanation: This evaluation question tests professional ethics under RA 9266 — the architect's non-delegable duty to refuse to seal non-compliant plans, regardless of client instructions.
questions.code_citation: BP 344 2024 IRR, Appendix A; RA 9266, Sec. 33
